Name: Ai (et-Tell) (העי (א-תל))
Description: A large open-air reservoir in Area K, exceeding 1800 cubic meters in volume, 25m wide, and 2.5m deep. It was designed to collect runoff water from the upper city via channels, featuring a stone floor on clay and a thick dam wall, dating to EB 1-3. The only known instance of plaster from this period is from a water pool at Ai, where impermeable clayey soil was used as a hydraulic material to line the reservoir.

Name: Barqa (ברקת)
Description: The site shows evidence of rainwater storage in soft chalk bedrock, indicating the use of rock-cut cisterns during the Early Bronze Age.

Name: Ein Qadis (עין קדיס)
Description: A permanent spring in the Western Negev Highlands, serving as a crucial water source around which Early Bronze Age settlements were concentrated.

Name: Jawa (ג'ווה)
Description: Three water collection systems and two modified natural pools (P3, P4) with a total capacity of 1800 cubic meters. The system involved diverting water from Wadi Rajil with a diversion dam and channels to fill the pools, dated to the Early Bronze Age.

Name: Kadesh Barnea (Ein el-Gudeirat) (קדש ברנע (עין אל-קודייראת))
Description: A permanent spring in the Western Negev Highlands, serving as a crucial water source around which Early Bronze Age settlements were concentrated.

Name: Khirbet Zeiraqoun (חירבת זירקון)
Description: Three stepped shafts were excavated, leading to a groundwater level approximately 60m deep. One shaft is 100m long, reaching the bottom of Wadi Shallala. Horizontal tunnels and connecting stepped tunnels were proposed to bring water into the city, dated to EB 2-3.

Name: Mezer (מצר)
Description: Multiple rock-cut cisterns, including a large one (B3) 5m deep and another (D7) with niches, were used for rainwater collection via rock-cut channels. These cisterns were unplastered due to the impermeable Nari and chalk bedrock.

Name: Midiya (מידיא)
Description: This Early Bronze Age settlement, like others in Western Samaria, utilized unplastered cisterns carved into soft chalk bedrock to collect rainwater, compensating for the absence of nearby springs.

Name: Nahal Horasha Illit (Well) (נחל חורשה עילי (באר))
Description: A well near Mount Ramon, possibly originating in the Early Bronze Age (or even Pre-Pottery Neolithic) when the water table was higher, despite its later Ottoman reconstruction.

Name: Ovda Valley (בקעת עובדה)
Description: Four wells were discovered, cut into a water-bearing layer. One well, well-preserved, has a 1.5-1m opening, is bell-shaped, 1.5m deep, and lined with stones. Its dating to the Chalcolithic and Early Bronze Age is based on nearby flint tools. Two methods of water storage were identified: 'granot' (runoff collection basins), dams, and depressions in clay, in addition to wells. These systems were associated with Early Bronze Age 2 settlement clusters.

Name: Shabtin (שבתין)
Description: This Early Bronze Age settlement, located near a spring, also featured unplastered cisterns carved into soft chalk bedrock for rainwater collection, a common practice in Western Samaria.

Name: Tel Arad (תל ערד)
Description: A well is located in the heart of the Early Bronze Age city. Although re-used in the Iron Age, it is suggested that its initial excavation dates to the Early Bronze Age as part of a larger runoff water collection system. An open-air pool/reservoir in the city center, formed by collecting rainwater runoff through radial streets into a natural depression, covering about one dunam. Water collection from rooftops into large pithoi is also suggested for this EB city. Arad had central water pools for collecting runoff, and large storage jars (pithoi) were used within houses for water storage. Clayey soil was used as a hydraulic plaster for water installations.

Name: Tel Bet Yerah (בית ירח)
Description: A basalt-lined tunnel, roofed with basalt slabs, was discovered on the southern edge of Tel Bet Yerah. It is interpreted as part of an Early Bronze Age III water system, possibly an aqueduct bringing water from mountain springs or a channel collecting runoff within the city.

Name: Tel Dalit (תל דלית)
Description: A fortified Early Bronze Age settlement with several rock-cut cisterns in soft chalk bedrock, designed to collect rainwater. One examined cistern was irregular, 2.2m deep to the chamber, with a rectangular chamber 2.6x2.0m, showing no signs of plaster due to the impermeable chalk. Shallow wells in nearby wadis likely supplemented water supply during peacetime.

Name: Tel Megiddo (תל מגידו)
Description: Despite massive city walls, an Early Bronze Age water system was likely present, possibly a depression in the northern part of the tel, though specific details are scarce due to later archaeological layers.

Name: Tel Mizpon le-Fahma (תל מצפון לפחמה)
Description: This Early Bronze Age settlement, like others in Western Samaria, utilized unplastered cisterns carved into soft chalk bedrock to collect rainwater, compensating for the absence of nearby springs.

Name: Tel near Bazariya (תל ליד בזריה)
Description: This Early Bronze Age settlement, like others in Western Samaria, utilized unplastered cisterns carved into soft chalk bedrock to collect rainwater, compensating for the absence of nearby springs.

Name: Tel Yarmut (תל ירמות)
Description: Although no formal water system has been discovered for the Early Bronze Age, a clear topographical depression at the lowest point of the 150-dunam city likely served to collect runoff water.

Name: Tepe Gawra (טפה גאורה)
Description: Two wells were found. The older well (Layer VIIIb, Late Uruk/EB) was 2.8m in diameter, excavated to 24m, plastered with mud, and featured steps, connected to a bitumen-lined drainage channel. A second well (Layer VI, early 3rd millennium BCE) also had a drainage channel leading to it.
